prompt.es: Escucha el informe y elige qué da a entender el tutor sobre cómo debería estudiar Mia.

choices.text: She should reread every draft twice to catch the slips before handing it in.
She should drill the increase of prices, which is her only recurring error.
She should put her effort into the repeated errors instead of the slips.
She should ask him to mark fewer slips in her next drafts.

feedback.es: El tutor resta importancia a los descuidos y pide un diagnóstico de los errores recurrentes: eso orienta la prioridad de estudio de Mia.

origin.audio: Mia's tutor has just finished marking her last four drafts. Fourteen marks in total, he says, but only six of them are careless slips: a dropped article here, a missing plural there, the kind of thing Mia corrects herself as soon as she reads them again. The other eight are different. Three times she wrote the increase of prices, twice she added but after much as, and three times she opened a request with a direct question. According to the tutor, nobody should lose sleep over the slips, whereas the recurring errors deserve a proper diagnosis, because they show rules she has never really absorbed.

prompt.es: ¿Qué actitud muestra Tom ante las correcciones que ha recibido?

choices.text: He is grateful, but doubts that the marks describe his real weakness.
He is pleased that the marks confirm what he thought about vocabulary.
He is discouraged and thinks he will never sound natural in writing.
He is surprised, but ready to change his study plan because of the marks.

feedback.es: Tom dice que esperaba un problema de vocabulario y que las marcas cuentan otra historia; empieza un registro de correcciones, lo que revela sorpresa y disposición a cambiar de plan.

origin.text: Hi Ana, thanks for marking my drafts. I had assumed that my main weakness was vocabulary, but the marks tell a different story: nearly all of them concern how I sound rather than what I say. I have started keeping a log of my corrections, and I intend to bring it to our next session in case it helps us decide where to begin.

prompt.es: Completa: «Leo la ayudó a rastrear el error hasta su causa de fondo.»

answer.text: root

feedback.es: Root cause es la colocación para el origen real de un problema; detrás de la repetición hay una causa, aquí la traducción literal.

origin.text: The same error appeared in every one of Ana's drafts. When Leo helped her trace it back to its ___ cause, she saw that it was a blind spot: she had been copying a Spanish pair of linking words into English word for word.

prompt.es: Diagnostica en inglés: nombra la categoría del error y la regla que rompe.

answer.text: This is a register slip. After a noun of change such as drop, the thing that changes takes in, so the correct phrase is the drop in prices.
accepted: This is a register slip. After a noun of change such as drop, the thing that changes takes in, so the correct phrase is the drop in prices.
It is an academic register error: drop needs in, not of, so we should say the drop in prices.
This is a slip of register. A noun of change like drop is followed by in, so it should be the drop in prices.

feedback.es: Un buen diagnóstico nombra la categoría (registro), enuncia la regla (in tras un sustantivo de cambio) y da la frase corregida.

origin.text: La frase marcada en el borrador de Leo es: «The drop of prices worried the managers.» Explica de qué categoría es el error y cuál es la frase correcta.

prompt.es: ¿Con qué propósito escribe la autora este párrafo?

choices.text: To argue that repeated mistakes need a named rule, not merely more attention.
To warn learners that careless slips cost more marks than recurring errors.
To reassure learners that repeated marks disappear once they write more.
To describe how one learner improved her writing over a single term.

feedback.es: La autora rechaza la idea de que el problema sea la falta de cuidado y defiende que una regla sin nombre seguirá produciendo la misma marca.

origin.text: Most learners read their corrections and promise to be more careful, which is precisely the wrong lesson. Care is not the issue. A sentence such as the increase of prices worried us is not careless; it simply reflects a rule that was never absorbed. Until that rule has a name, no amount of attention will stop the same mark from returning in the next draft.

origin.text: Academic writers prefer nouns to verbs. Instead of saying that prices fell sharply, they refer to the sharp ___ in prices, and that small change is enough to raise the register of the sentence.

es: Reparar con el mínimo cambio frases con errores de gramática oral, concesión, contingencia, registro y narración, y decidir cuánto hay que tocar para conservar la voz del autor.

prompt.es: ¿Qué critica la tutora de la corrección que hizo Tom?

choices.text: That he left the main error in the second clause as it was.
That he replaced formal wording with a much more casual style.
That he missed the shift in tense that she had flagged.
That he changed more of the text than the errors required.

feedback.es: La tutora dice que cambió seis palabras cuando solo dos fallaban y que una buena reparación conserva la voz del autor: critica el exceso de cambios.

origin.text: Your repaired version changes six words, yet only two of them were wrong. The original clause, Should sales falls, was nearly right: once the extra s is removed, nothing else needs to change. You did not have to rewrite it as If sales were to fall. A good repair fixes the rule and keeps the voice of the writer, so next time flag the error, swap out one word and stop.

prompt.es: Escucha a la editora y elige qué postura adopta ante la norma del manual.

choices.text: She accepts the rule for formal documents but resists applying it everywhere.
She regrets the rule and would like to see it removed from the guide.
She supports the rule in every document because it is short and formal.
She wants contracts to use a plain if and emails to use should.

feedback.es: La editora ve la lógica de la norma para contratos e informes, pero defiende un if sencillo en correos: acepta la norma con reservas.

origin.audio: When we drafted our style guide last spring, several of us argued for a single pattern, and I was one of them. The guide now says that every contingency clause must begin with should, and I still see the logic: the pattern is short and formal. In an email to a colleague, though, Should it rain, the match will be postponed can sound stiff. I would keep the rule for contracts and reports, and leave emails free to use a plain if. Asking every reader to accept one pattern would only make our writing less natural. Having tested it on real emails, I have changed my mind.

prompt.es: ¿Qué da a entender el autor sobre la reparación más formal posible?

choices.text: That formal repairs should be avoided in every kind of message.
That the most formal version is not always the best choice for the reader.
That teammates dislike correct sentences that contain should.
That a repair should keep the wording as close to the original as possible.

feedback.es: El autor admite que la frase es correcta y precisa, pero fría para unos compañeros: lo formal no siempre es lo mejor para el lector.

origin.text: A repaired sentence that reads as if a committee had written it is not a good repair. Consider Should it rain, the match will be postponed. It is formal, precise and correct, yet in a message to teammates it would sound cold. The skill lies in matching the wording to the reader, not in applying the strictest rule available.

es: Interpretar el lenguaje figurado y lo implícito en una letra breve: distinguir lo que dicen las palabras de lo que sugieren y justificar el tono con palabras concretas.

teaching.en: In song lyrics, figurative language works through metaphor: a paper boat on a grey river is never literal.
teaching.es: En las letras de canciones, el lenguaje figurado funciona mediante la metáfora: un barquito de papel en un río gris nunca es literal.
teaching.explanationEs: Lo literal es lo que dicen las palabras; lo figurado, lo que quieren decir. Una imagen imposible o rara suele pedir lectura figurada.

teaching.en: To read between the lines, ask what the singer avoids saying, because the lyrics often imply more than any single verse states.
teaching.es: Para leer entre líneas, pregúntate qué evita decir la cantante, porque la letra suele dar a entender más de lo que afirma cualquier estrofa.
teaching.explanationEs: Imply: la letra sugiere algo que nunca dice con todas las letras; lo que se calla también comunica.

teaching.en: A hint of regret can sit inside a cheerful verse: the singer says I am fine, yet the tone quietly contradicts her.
teaching.es: Un matiz de pesar puede esconderse en una estrofa alegre: la cantante dice «estoy bien», pero el tono la contradice sin alzar la voz.
teaching.explanationEs: El tono (suave, irónico, resignado) se deduce de las palabras elegidas y de lo que no encaja con ellas.

teaching.en: A faint echo in an empty room can evoke absence, since a sound that returns without an answer suggests that someone has left.
teaching.es: Un eco tenue en una habitación vacía puede evocar ausencia, porque un sonido que vuelve sin respuesta sugiere que alguien se ha ido.
teaching.explanationEs: Un sonido o un espacio vacío insinúan una ausencia sin nombrarla.
segments: A faint echo in an empty room can evoke absence, since a
sound that returns without an answer suggests that someone has left.

origin.audio: The final verse of Last Bus Home is only four lines long. The singer folds a timetable into her pocket, turns off the hall light and says, to the empty hall, that some doors are better left unlocked. Nothing in the verse mentions the person who left. Critics have noticed that the word tomorrow appears in every verse except this one, and that its absence makes the ending feel quieter, less hopeful and more final. Yet the unlocked door suggests that the singer has not entirely given up. It is, the host concludes, a song that refuses to explain itself, and that is exactly why people keep arguing about it.

feedback.es: El crítico contrasta la lectura habitual (una canción triste sobre una ruptura) con la suya (paciencia más que pérdida): propone una interpretación menos evidente.

origin.text: Some listeners hear Last Bus Home as a sad song about a break-up. I hear something less obvious: the singer never blames anyone, and the simple language she uses keeps the feeling in check. Sadness, here, is handled like weather: noticed, described, accepted. It is a song about patience more than loss.

She stopped there and said that the student had not written the word lonely once, yet every reader had felt it. She added, however, that the ending spoiled everything: the bus stopped, the man stepped off, and the writer explained in three sentences what the story had meant. prompt.es: Escribe tu relato (180–300 palabras): escena, ritmo, giro, final e ironía.

answer.text: Rain tapped the window of the night bus. Tom counted his coins twice, and then a third time, while his foot beat the floor. Behind him, a man in a grey suit sighed at his own watch. On Tom's knees lay the folder with his drawings, and his hands would not stay still. The driver hummed a cheerful song, which made everything worse. Off the bus he jumped, and up the stairs he ran. Silence in the corridor. A closed door. He was sure he had missed the interview by ten minutes, and he had practised his speech all week. Then a woman appeared at the end of the hall, holding a cup of tea. "Are you Tom?" she asked. "We had to postpone everything. The director, of course, is stuck in traffic." Tom laughed so loudly that the secretary looked up. It turned out that the director had been sitting behind him on the bus all along, and he arrived five minutes later, out of breath, blaming the driver's song. In the end, Tom got the job, and the driver got a thank-you card.
accepted: Rain tapped the window of the night bus. Tom counted his coins twice, and then a third time, while his foot beat the floor. Behind him, a man in a grey suit sighed at his own watch. On Tom's knees lay the folder with his drawings, and his hands would not stay still. The driver hummed a cheerful song, which made everything worse. Off the bus he jumped, and up the stairs he ran. Silence in the corridor. A closed door. He was sure he had missed the interview by ten minutes, and he had practised his speech all week. Then a woman appeared at the end of the hall, holding a cup of tea. "Are you Tom?" she asked. "We had to postpone everything. The director, of course, is stuck in traffic." Tom laughed so loudly that the secretary looked up. It turned out that the director had been sitting behind him on the bus all along, and he arrived five minutes later, out of breath, blaming the driver's song. In the end, Tom got the job, and the driver got a thank-you card.

Every Sunday my grandfather fished at the lake, and every Sunday he came home with an empty bucket and a happy face. My mother laughed and said that fishing was only an excuse to sit in silence. One morning I followed him. Into the water went his line, and out of the silence came nothing. Hours passed. Nobody spoke, and even the gulls seemed to be waiting for something to happen. The lake stayed as still as a painting. Then a tiny silver fish jumped into the bucket by itself. My grandfather stared at it. His hands shook a little as he lifted the bucket. I had never seen him so excited, or so suspicious. "Of course," he said at last, "the day I bring a friend, the fish behave." It turned out that he had been hiding a secret all along: he had never caught a single fish, and he was delighted about it. In the end, he let the fish go and told everybody it was the best catch of his life. Since then, he has never fished alone.

answer.text: I would like to put forward a proposal for the open day: a story workshop in the square. By last spring, the square had been empty for months, and many neighbours told me they missed a place to meet. A workshop with a small book stall could change that. The square belongs to all of us, and a story is the cheapest way to fill it. I know that a new idea always raises questions, and I welcome them, because a fair point can only improve the plan. I understand that the budget is tight, and much as I appreciate your concern, I believe we can manage. I was wondering whether the volunteers could bring the books and the chairs, so the cost would be almost nothing, and nobody would need to spend money on anything else. Should it rain, we will move the workshop into the hall. Failing that, we can shorten the morning. If everyone agrees, I will confirm the stall by Friday, and by Saturday we will have prepared the posters. Shall we agree on that? Thank you for listening, and I hope you will join us.

Let me put forward a proposal: a story workshop for the open day. When I was a child, the square used to be full of people, and I would love to see that again. Stories can bring neighbours together, and a simple workshop is a good way to start. I also believe that a workshop like this costs very little and gives a lot back. Nobody needs a big stage to tell a story, only a few chairs and a little time. Fair enough, the budget is limited. Much as I would like a bigger stall, I am sure the volunteers can help, and I was wondering whether the library could lend us some books for the morning. In the event of rain, the workshop will take place in the hall. By Friday I will have confirmed the stall with the council, and the posters will be ready by Saturday. That is our deadline, and I am confident that we can meet it together. Are we all happy with this plan? Thank you for listening, and I hope that many of you will come and tell a story of your own.

I would like to propose a workshop where neighbours write a short story together, one sentence each. The idea came from last year, when a stranger left a notebook on a bench and within a week the whole street had filled it. I understand that some of you worry about the noise and the cost, and I accept that both are fair points. Much as I am keen on the idea, I would not want it to divide us. I was wondering whether we could try it for one morning, with a small stall and a handful of volunteers, and then decide. Should the weather turn bad, we can use the library. By Friday I will have spoken to the volunteers, and by the following Friday we will have a clear answer. If the morning goes badly, at least we will have tried. I am not asking for a big budget, only for one morning and a little goodwill from all of us. Does that seem a fair compromise? Thank you for listening, and please tell me what you think before we vote.
